section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section provides the date and occasion for the maamar.
section.t: With the help of Heaven.
Motzaei Shabbos Parshas Vayeitzei,
the 9th of Kislev,
the eve of the 10th of Kislev,
the year 5739*

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that "He redeemed in peace" means the redemption occurs through the complete nullification of the opponent, without war, and questions how this applies when one is amidst battles.
section.t: "He redeemed my soul in peace from the battle that was against me, for many were with me."
And the Baal HaGeulah explains in his discourse beginning with these words
(printed in his book Shaarei Teshuvah)
that the explanation of "He redeemed in peace"
(specifically in peace)
is that the redemption is in a manner that the opponent is completely nullified,
so that there is no need for war at all.
And this is analogous to what was in the days of Shlomo,
that all the nations were nullified before Shlomo without war,
therefore he was called Shlomo because there was peace in his days.
And he makes a precise point in the discourse,
that when one is in a state where there are no opponents at all,
why is redemption needed?
And one can say the explanation of this precision,
for the explanation of "He redeemed in peace" is not that peace comes after the redemption
(i.e., that the redemption is through war and afterwards there is peace),
but rather,
that the redemption
(itself)
is in peace,
and therefore he makes the precise point,
that in a state of peace there seemingly is no need for redemption.
And one can add another precision,
that in this same verse it is written "He redeemed... from the battle that was against me,"
that this redemption of my soul is from the wars that come upon me,
and how can it be that the redemption from wars is a redemption in peace,
for seemingly they are two opposite matters.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that these two concepts are not just opposites but extreme opposites, and describes how the most intense war involves closeness and grappling.
section.t: B)
And one can add,
that these two matters
("He redeemed in peace" and "from the battle that was against me")
are not merely two opposites
(simply),
but rather they are opposites from one extreme to the other.
For, behold, the reason that war is called "krav" from the term "kiruv" (closeness)
(even though war is the opposite of closeness),
is
(as understood from the discourse),
because the essence and intensity of war is when it is in a manner of closeness.
For, behold, in war there are two modes.
That the two combatants are at a distance from each other,
and they throw
(at one another)
stones, arrows, catapults, and the like.
Or that the two combatants draw close to each other
(in proximity of place)
until they grapple with each other,
"And a man wrestled with him,"
that they draw close to each other
(not only in place,
but)
also in their bodies,
to the point that the two combatants embrace each other.
And this war
(the ultimate closeness)
is the most difficult war.
